How to plan a container load, with a worked example

Before you book space, you want to know how many cartons or pallets go in a container, and how many containers the whole load needs. The answer is set by four things: the floor area, how many layers fit under the roof, what you may stack on what, and the payload limit. Whichever runs out first sets the count.

Open the free container load planner

The four limits

Floor. Count how many footprints fit across the width and along the length, trying both ways round. Odd widths waste floor: two 120 cm Euro pallets side by side do not fit a 235 cm interior, so loaders mix pallet directions, and that is what a packer has to search for.

Layers. Divide the inside height by the unit height, rounded down. A 110 cm pallet gets two layers under a 239 cm roof and wastes 19 cm; an 85 cm pallet gets two layers in a standard 40 ft and three in a high cube, because three times 85 is 255 and the high cube is about 270 cm tall.

Stacking. Cartons marked fragile or pallets of soft goods may not be stacked, so the layer count becomes one. The planner takes a highest layer and a weight allowed on top for each line.

Payload. A dense load fills the payload before the space. A 600 kg pallet in a 26,500 kg container stops at 44 pallets however much air is left.

A worked example

An invented exporter has 150 Euro pallets, each 120 × 80 × 85 cm and 250 kg, which may be stacked. The planner uses nominal inside sizes of 12,032 × 2,352 × 2,393 mm for a 40 ft container and 2,698 mm high for the high cube, both with a 26,500 kg payload. These are commonly quoted figures, not a certificate for your equipment.

The floor takes 25 pallets in both, in a mixed arrangement of lengthwise and crosswise rows. The standard container stops at two layers, 50 pallets, so 150 pallets need three of them. The high cube takes a third layer, 75 pallets, so two of them carry everything, at 18,750 kg each, well inside the payload.

Change the pallet height to 110 cm and the extra height buys nothing: three layers need 330 cm, so a high cube still holds two layers and 50 pallets. Whether a high cube pays depends on the cargo, not on the container alone.

Now make the pallets 600 kg and 110 cm tall, 70 of them, in a standard 40 ft. The floor and the two layers would take 50, but the payload stops the first container at 44 pallets (26,400 kg); the remaining 26 pallets go in a second container, 15,600 kg. Two containers, and the lower bound from weight is also two.

What the planner does that a rule of thumb does not

  1. It packs mixed lines, so a pallet and four sizes of carton share one container and fill each other's gaps.
  2. It respects rotation: upright only, any orientation, or fixed as entered.
  3. It reports what is left over, how many containers the whole load needs, a lower bound from volume and weight, and a to-scale top and side view with a loading list.
  4. It compares every standard size, loose and on pallets, so the high cube and the pallet question get an answer for your own cargo.

It is a heuristic: it tries many orderings and keeps the best, which is not a proof that nothing better exists. A person who knows the cargo may find another fit, so keep a margin.

Common questions

How many pallets fit in a 20 ft container?

A nominal 20 ft container is about 5.9 m long and 2.35 m wide, so its floor holds about 11 Euro pallets or 10 of the 48 x 40 inch size, and a second layer doubles that if the pallets are low and strong enough to stack. The planner packs your own pallet size and weight rather than quoting a number.

Does a high cube container always hold more?

No. It adds about 30 cm of height, which helps only when a whole extra layer fits. Three layers of 85 cm pallets fit a high cube but not a standard container; three layers of 110 cm fit neither.

Why does weight sometimes decide the count?

A container has a payload limit. Dense goods such as 600 kg pallets reach it long before the space is used, so the number per container is the payload divided by the weight per unit, rounded down.

Should I palletise or load cartons loose?

Pallets are faster to load and handle, but each deck takes height and the pallet footprint can waste floor. Compare both on your own cargo; the planner's comparison table shows containers and fill for each.

Choosing carton sizes before you pack? The shipping box size optimizer picks which sizes to stock. Shipping a single pallet by LTL? The LTL freight class estimator works out the class.

How it is calculated

Packing: a constructive 3D bin packing heuristic with extreme-point placement. Units go in one at a time at the lowest free corner where they are inside the walls, overlap nothing, and rest on the floor or on units below with at least 75% of their base supported. Each is slid back against the walls and neighbours. The search repeats with three corner rules and several unit orderings, including seeded random ones, and keeps the packing with the most packed volume, then the most units. It is repeatable: the same input gives the same plan.

Constraints: allowed rotations, highest layer, weight allowed on top (spread over the units underneath in proportion to the area they carry) and the payload limit. A separate checker re-verifies every plan for bounds, overlap, payload, orientation, support, layers and load before it is drawn.

Whole load: one container at a time, then what is left, then an attempt to merge the last two. The lower bound is the larger of total volume over container volume and total weight over payload.

Not modelled: load securing and bracing, axle and gross weights, centre of gravity, pallet overhang, dunnage and gaps for lashing, door and forklift clearances, hazardous or temperature-controlled goods, carrier or legal limits, and rates. Container sizes and payloads are nominal figures you can edit; check your equipment. Unverified against a real loading: tested on hand-computed fits and on random loads checked for overlap, bounds, weight and rotation.

Common questions

How many pallets fit in a 40 ft container?

It depends on the pallet size, its height and whether it may be stacked. Euro pallets (120 x 80 cm) fit about 25 on the floor of a nominal 40 ft container, in a mix of lengthwise and crosswise rows, so about 50 if they can be stacked two high; 48 x 40 inch pallets fit about 20 on the floor. A nominal 20 ft container takes about 11 Euro pallets or 10 of the 48 x 40 size on the floor. Enter your own pallet size, weight and stacking limit and the planner packs it rather than quoting a rule of thumb.

How does the planner pack a container?

It is a constructive 3D bin packing heuristic. Units are placed one at a time at the lowest free corner where they stay inside the walls, overlap nothing, rest on the floor or on units below with at least 75 percent of the base supported, respect the rotations each line allows, and keep the weight under the payload. Each placement is slid against the walls and neighbours. The search repeats that with different corner rules and unit orderings, including seeded random ones, and keeps the packing with the most volume, then the most units.

Is this the best possible packing?

Not guaranteed. Optimal 3D packing is an NP-hard problem, so the planner is a heuristic that tries many orderings and keeps the best; on regular loads it often finds a perfect fit, on awkward mixes it can leave a little room that a skilled loader would use. Treat the unit counts as a planning estimate and keep a margin.

What do upright only, can rotate and highest layer mean?

Upright only keeps the height you entered vertical and lets the unit turn on its vertical axis. Can rotate allows all six orientations. Fixed keeps the unit exactly as entered. Highest layer is the highest level a unit may sit at, with 1 meaning floor only. Weight allowed on top is the most weight that may rest on one unit, counting everything above it; 0 means nothing may be put on it.

How many containers do I need for the whole load?

The planner fills one container at a time, then repeats on what is left, and reports the number of containers, how full each is, and a lower bound from total volume and total weight. It then tries to merge the last two containers into one. Because it is a heuristic the count may be one higher than the best possible; the lower bound shows how close it is.

What does swapping to a 40 ft high cube or to pallets change?

The comparison runs the same cargo through every standard size and through pallets. A high cube adds height, which helps only if your units can stack. Palletising packs your cartons onto 48 x 40 inch pallets within a height cap, then packs the loaded pallets into each container; it usually costs some volume to the pallet deck but makes the load faster to handle. The table shows the container count and fill for each so you can weigh it against your own quotes.

Does this check that my load is safe or legal?

No. It is a planning aid. It does not check load securing, axle weights, centre of gravity, pallet overhang, hazardous goods rules, or any road, rail, sea or air limit, and it uses nominal container sizes that you can edit. Your carrier, forwarder or loading supervisor decides what can be shipped.

Is my cargo list uploaded?

No. The planner runs in your browser from figures you type, nothing is sent to a server, there are no accounts, and it works offline after the page loads.
